merge_history.rationale: Hazebrouck cloth spellings folded into cloth's `hazebrouck` locational qualifier; the stone sense of `hasborough` split off to new entry `hasborough stone`.

granum_2 was a duplicate of the kermes/scarlet-grain dyestuff sense; absorbed into granum. The conflated grains-of-paradise spice qualifiers (paradisi, garble-of-paradise) were split out to `greynes`.
Consolidated the woad dyestuff (Isatis tinctoria) and its grade-entries; wood-confusion senses moved to `wood`.
Timber sense of lignum + woode folded into wood; lignum split into lignum aloes / lignum vitae.
Sifted grenes into the green-cloth concept; disguised green-X qualifiers relocated (dornick gets a grene qualifier; green woad/ginger already covered; greenstone split to its own entry).
Sifted grenes into the green-cloth concept; disguised green-X qualifiers relocated (dornick gets a grene qualifier; green woad/ginger already covered; greenstone split to its own entry).
Condensed 143 hat qualifiers; split bonde/bande->hatbonde, cardes->hatters carde, ferri->helm.
hammer's 'haft' qualifier (hammer haft) merged into the haft concept as a hammer-variant qualifier.
Split riding hammer from the hammer entry as a separate (war-hammer?) concept carrying all hammer spelling variants.
hawke 'belles' qualifier folded into existing hawk bell; laver/glove qualifiers became hawk laver and hawking glove.
Untangled horn cluster: core material kept in horn; drinking horn (from horn_2), drum, shoehorn created; type/worked senses routed to existing concepts; horn_3 kept as unidentified bucket.
Untangled horn cluster: core material kept in horn; drinking horn (from horn_2), drum, shoehorn created; type/worked senses routed to existing concepts; horn_3 kept as unidentified bucket.

Routed object-qualifiers off ivory (material) into existing concepts: 'comb' (ivory comb), 'haft' (ivory handle), 'elephant tusks' (ivory in form of tusks / de peciis dencium); each gains an 'ivory'+variants qualifier. Kept quality qualifiers (operatum, reffutz) on ivory. Consolidated comb's scattered ivory spelling-variant qualifiers into one.

Split conflated javelin attestations into composite parts per EB note: javelin (complete spear/dart) keeps casteng/with-head/without-head/parvi qualifiers; new related concepts javelin head (metal) and javelin stave (wooden shaft) carry the part attestations (e.g. javelinge stave/staves, javling heade). De-doubled the corrupted 'cum capite' concatenated forms.

Re-keyed 'jenete grey' -> 'jenet' (the genet / civet-cat fur). Stripped colour, pelles/pellis and dressing-state out of the compounded forms and into qualifiers (blak|nigri, grey|gray, pelles|pellis, rawe, tawid, untawid); atomised compound qualifiers (gray rawe, raw grey, pelles tawid grey). Bare spelling stems retained with their source IDs.

Removed the muddled male-gyrfalcon ('gyrkin/jerkin hawk') sense from the jerkin (garment) entry — dropped the bird description clause and the 'hawk' qualifier; those attestations already live under 'gyrfalcon'. Atomised the garment compound forms (X of lether, basell/bazell X) into bare spelling stems plus qualifiers (lether, basell, shepeskins).

Merged 'justing sadille' into 'sadele' (saddle) as a 'jousting' qualifier (per EB memo). Cloned the full cartesian product of jousting spellings (justing|justyng) x saddle spellings as forms; the four genuine attestations retain their source IDs (33, 1), synthetic recall-combos carry none. Latin sella/cella, the hakeney-saddle compounds and the stray cross-ref were excluded from the cartesian.

Major cleanup of kerchief: atomised ~55 duplicated/compound qualifiers into 25 atoms (places, materials, quality, size, age) with pipe-grouped spelling variants; dropped the propagated bogus 'fili -> Foca' annotation and empty placeholder anns, keeping the resolved ones (Cyprus, Valencia, Boulogne, silk, small). Atomised compound forms (X parys, X cotoni, X cours, X cipers) into bare stems + qualifiers; cotone is now part of the cotton qualifier. Merged the empty 'kerchief cotton' stub.

Consolidated 10 near-identical descriptions to one; atomised the qualifier list (grouped spelling variants, split compounds like 'densher narow', 'whyt northen', 'largus albus' into atoms by category); cleaned junk folio-number list from the 'album' gloss; split the two concatenated multi-term forms. Reinterpreted bare whyt/whytt as white not Isle of Wight (flagged for review).

Merged 'keveryng for a bed' (botched 'covering' for a bed) into bedclothes (AAT bed coverings). Forms carried over (keveryng for a bed, keveryng, kyboryng); compound forms atomised into qualifiers (verder=verdure, cum filler). Related to coverlet and coveryng.

Disentangled the kip (bundle of furs/hides, OED kip n.1) and kyppe/kipe (basket, MED kipe n.) homonyms: each description now describes only its own sense; moved the canonical basket spellings (kipe, kipes, kype) from kip to kyppe; assigned AAT (bundles+measures for kip, baskets for kyppe) and cross-linked the two as confusable. Form-level split flagged as context-dependent (helpWanted).

Consolidated 9 overlapping pipe/pipa/pype fragments into 4 concepts (per user): pipe (capacity measure/cask), pipe (instrument), pipe (weight)=½ dolium ponderis, and gold pipe (gold-thread tubes). Forms pooled by sense with union of source IDs; the cask concept carries all measure/packing sources as the dominant sense. AAT left for curation (helpWanted).

Consolidated ~19 paper fragments (per user): paper (material) + paper (measure) [OED 6b]; folded printing/writing/pressing/packing/venes paper and carta_2 into paper as qualifiers; kept printed paper and paynted paper as distinct print commodities. Forms pooled with union source IDs; printed/painted qualifiers routed to their concepts. AAT: paper(fiber) on material.

Re-added gold pipe as a clean concept attested as pipa auri / pipe auri (no qualifiers); removed the 'auri' qualifier from pipe accordingly. aurum Colonie / coper gold / de luka remain pipe qualifiers (measure of gilt-metal thread).

Split lace: kept the cord/lacing sense (OED lace n.3), atomised material/origin/colour/shape qualifiers, collapsed ~15 repetitive descriptions; routed the passement (gold/silver gimp/braid) qualifier-spellings (percemana, parcemyn, parcement, parcemana, parsement, poemen) to the existing passemain concept. Cross-linked lace with passemain, point, scholas, aglett.

Re-keyed lache de ferro pro crosbowys -> crossbow latch (iron release mechanism). Tidied lath: routed its crossbow-combined forms/qualifiers (pro crosbowis, crosbow, de stile) to the existing limb concept crossbow lath_2, and the naylle (lath-nail) qualifier to nail as a 'lath' qualifier with all lath spelling variants. lath now the plain wood-strip sense.

Pulled the lath-nail qualifier out of nail and merged it into the canonical 'lath nail' concept (rekeyed from lathnayle), populating the full lath x nail cross-product of spelling variants as concatenated forms.

Rekeyed laton->latten; consolidated genuine latten qualifiers (foil/plate/wire/colour/thickness/objects/uses) and removed contamination (goldbeater's skin, textiles, paper, stone, wood, iron/copper plate-wire, redundant latten-word qualifiers). Qualifiers carried no sources; all form sources retained.

Consolidated the pot fragments (stub + pot_2/3/4/5) into pot (vessel) + pot (measure) [user-chosen split]; extracted pot hanger as a distinct concept and removed it from the pot stub's description; routed potash (asshes/cinis) to pot ashes. ~150 qualifiers atomised by material/state/size/use and by capacity. Forms pooled with union sources; named pots (beer/chamber/melting/stew/pint pot/potelle etc.) left separate.

Split the muddled 'lam' entry: lambfell/lambskin merged into 'lame'; 'lam' kept for the white Welsh cloth; new 'lame (armour)' for the vague armour sense. Cross-linked lambz ficches to fitches and lame.

Consolidated 8 wool-fibre fragments into canonical 'wool' with origin/grade qualifiers; routed the wool-card sense to wul card and cotton wool to cotton; dropped sourceless lanolin-oil and wool-belt qualifiers (flagged for EB). Forms pooled with union sources.

Refined lasche: moved spelling-variant qualifiers (lashe/lasshe) to forms; atomised compound forms (pellis rede lashe, rubeum) into qualifiers; cross-linked to redlasshe. Red-dyewood sense and 'laces' flagged for further sifting.

Merged duplicate redlasshe (red cordovan leather) into lasche as one lasch/redlash concept with red/black qualifiers; atomised space-separated red-compounds, kept lexicalised redlash forms; reused cordwain's cordovan AAT. Routed 'laces' to lace. Dropped the sourceless red-dyewood muddle (flagged).

Merged lasing point into point (same concept — a tagged lace/cord for fastening clothing; lacing point = a point). Consolidated ~16 repetitive descriptions; atomised lasing-compound forms into the lasing|lasyng|lacyng qualifier with sources carried; cleaned junk 'see also poyntes' form. Related to aglett and longpoint.

Rekeyed leade->lead (the metal) and merged the duplicate plumbum (Latin lead). Split the white-lead pigment into a new 'white lead' concept, merging in plumbe blanke; routed the red-lead attestations to the existing 'red lead'. Source IDs preserved.

Merged lectum i (Latin lectus = a bed with its hangings) and bed tapestry into bed hangings; atomised the combined qualifier list; routed the featherbed sense (plumarum/de plumis) to featherbed; related to tester, valance, celure, featherbed.

Refined lettuis (snow-weasel fur / lettice): split the concatenated 'letwes letowes leticia' qualifier into forms; deduped qualifiers; consolidated descriptions; atomised spaced 'letow werk' (kept concatenated werk-forms).

Unified padlock + padlock_2 (AAT padlocks); absorbed the hanging-lock attestations and routed lock's hanging/hangyng/henging/pendens qualifiers here (hanging lock = padlock). Tidied lock and related the two.
Merged lyer into liere (same concept: lioure, binding tape for fabric edges; lyer's own cited MED definition matches liere). Atomised lyor pro lectis into a pro lectis qualifier.

Merged long skeyn into skene (both = skein, a measure of thread/yarn on a reel; OED skein n.1). 'long' becomes a qualifier (the standardized long skein, c=120 lb, BoR 39); long-skein sources carried via bare skein-spellings + the concatenated 'longskayn' form.

Merged the duplicate chest_2 (measure entry with identical forms) and ship cista into chest; atomised the combined qualifiers (size/half/single/sugar/Cyprus/Prussia/empty/iron-bound/uses/ship); kept chests + weights-and-measures AAT. Related to coffer, forcer_2.

Split the muddled 'lyne' entry: the lime/linden-board sense -> new 'lyneboard' (also pulling board's lyne/de lynde qualifiers there); the ship-line (cable) sense -> 'line' (flax/linen thread + ship line). Tidied lynen cloth and flagged the ambiguous 'wyght'.

De-coupled mace: kept 'mace' as the spice (mace n.2); split the sceptre/staff-of-office and iron-weapon senses (mace n.1) into 'mace (sceptre)', to which brugges golde / silver / iorn resolve; absorbed the weapon-mace 'mas' there. Split the missal sense (mas boke) into 'missal'. 'mase' (Normandy glass measure) left untouched.
Split obviously-polysemous 'roba' into distinct concepts ['roba', 'robe'] (conservative review pass).
Split obviously-polysemous 'vitar' into distinct concepts ['vitar', 'vitry'] (conservative review pass).

Merged nutt+nux nucis into generic nut; split qualifiers to other commodities (nutmeg/hazelnut already cover muscata/avelana; new nux vomica and nutcracker concepts). raptors->hawks(bird) on falcon/goshawk/gyrfalcon/laneret.
Consolidated 10 pack packing-unit fragments into pack (AAT packs); atomised size/measure qualifiers; routed pack-thread->packthrede, pack-needle->new pack needle, packduck->new packduck.
Consolidated 13 poke packing-unit fragments (incl. diminutive pokett/pokettus) into poke; bags AAT (suggested) carried; size/hops qualifiers atomised.
Consolidated 15 roll/rolla/rotulus fragments into roll; atomised size/use qualifiers; dropped suggested commodity AATs (buckram, wax).
Merged sack + sack_2 (same sack packing-unit/measure; flax + English-wool 364lb); atomised half/size qualifiers and the sacke-dimidii compound forms; kept sackette/sack bell/sack cloth separate.

Merged pocke into poke (base); created pocket from pokate+pockettus + the diminutive forms previously over-folded into poke; pulled pocke commodity qualifiers (nedille/threde/duke/canvas/shete) out to needle/packthrede/packduck/packing.
De-mixed pan(vessel)/pane(fur bundle)/panis(loaf measure); created sugar loaf; absorbed pan_2.
Atomised pannus 274 compound cloth qualifiers into 104 atoms; cross-linked to cloth.
Merge parchement+pergamenum into parchment; route lace->passement; reduce compound forms.
Pulled paten-nail sense out of nail (paten qualifier) and pattens (nail qualifier) into patene nayle.
Disambiguate bare cloth forms to cloth pictorum; connect to pannus depictus.
De-mix peper: spice (AAT pepper); pepper quern + pepper box split out; qualifiers grouped.
Merge pece+pecia (piece/measure); split leather-offcut sense into leather pieces.
Consolidated the 6 pecia/pece piece-measure fragments into pecia; dropped commodity AAT mis-tags; consolidated the commodity-measure descriptions.

q.d: Pure metallic element having symbol Au and atomic number 79; a soft, inert, shiny reddish yellow metal that is very malleable and ductile. Gold has been highly valued and found in artifacts dating to before 5000 BCE. Native gold, found in quartz veins (vein gold) and alluvial deposits (placer gold), generally contains some silver and copper. Gold is purified by dissolution in mercury or cyanide solutions, by melting, or by electrodeposition. The purity of commercial gold is expressed in karats which is the number of parts of gold in 24 parts of the alloy. Today gold is primarily used for monetary systems and for jewelry. [Source: Getty AAT]

agnus dei.d: Refers to disks of wax bearing the sign of the Agnus Dei, which is a symbol of Christ in the form of a lamb bearing a cross with a halo round its head. The small cake of wax was stamped with such a figure and blessed by the Pope. The wax may be the remains of the Pascal candle, solemnly blessed by the Pope on the Thursday after Easter. Disks may be round or oval. Figures of saints or the name and arms of the Pope are commonly impressed on the reverse. Agnus Deis may be worn suspended round the neck, or they may be preserved as objects of devotion. In virtue of the consecration they receive, they are regarded as "sacramentals," like holy water or blessed palms. [Source: Getty AAT]

alabaster.d: Fine-grained marblelike variety of gypsum that is easy to carve but is rather fragile; it has been used as a sculpture material, ornamental building work, vases, small decorative carvings, and powdered for use as a paper filler and paint pigment called mineral white or terra alba. Alabaster is usually a translucent white or pink but may also be a muted red, yellow or gray. It is soft and can be scratched slightly with a fingernail. It also dissolves slowly in wet environments. [Source: Getty AAT]

amber.d: A yellowish, hard, glassy, translucent fossil tree resin found in largest deposits on the Baltic coast and dating 40-60 million years old. Types of amber are classified by location. Amber is composed of complex mixtures of oxidized and polymerized resin acids and resin alcohols. It has been gathered or mined since Paleolithic times. It is easy to carve and was often used in its natural state for jewelry, beads, amulets, and small vessels. It was also used as an ingredient in paint; dark color oil and amber varnishes are made by dissolving melted amber in amber oil, turpentine oil, or a drying oil. It develops an electrical charge when rubbed with a cloth. It is also valued because very ancient insects and plants may be preserved in the amber. [Source: Getty AAT]

cast.memo: The development of cast is actually quite interesting. It comes from the Middle Dutch term "warp" (or the Low Germen term "werf" which means "to throw" i.e. in the case of pots it probably has something to do with the idea of throwing pots on the wheel. It was then translated into English as cast where by the mid-16th century it is primarily used as a quantity for pots. Particularly German stoneware. Basically until 1604 1 cast = 3 pots. It can also be seen used in the 15th century in Hull and Newcastle. As Jenks notes it was also used as a quantity of fish in limited cases. It was included in from the 1550s Book of Rates onwards. EB 26/02/2026.

copper.d: Pure metallic element having the symbol Cu and atomic number 29; a reddish brown, ductile metal that is present in the earth's crust, occurring as a native metal and as ores of sulfide, sulfate and carbonate (azurite, malachite, etc.). It was the first metal used by humans, probably from about 8000 BCE, in the regions of Mesopotamia and India. By about 3800 BCE copper was made into bronze for weapons and knives. Today, copper is one of the most widely used metals because it has high electrical and thermal conductivity, can be easily fabricated, is ductile and polishes well. In moist air, copper forms a protective green film of basic carbonate. Metallic copper combines well with other metals to form alloys, most commonly brass and bronze. Copper and its alloys are used for wire, electrical devices, pipes, cooking vessels, ammunition, ornamental trim, roofing, grillwork, coins, musical instruments, jewelry, and sculptures. [Source: Getty AAT]

flax.d: Fiber derived from the bast or skin of the stem of the species Linum usitatissimum. Soft, flexible fibers are produced by retting the stem of the flax plant, then washing and cleaning the fibers. Flax fibers of thinner and longer than cotton, but the fiber tube has thicker walls resulting in a stronger thread. Additionally, flax fibers are used for linen fabric, thread for making shoes and bookbinding, fish line, and twine. Waste flax fibers are used in banknotes, cigarette covers, and writing and drawing paper. [Source: Getty AAT]

gall.d: Material made of excrescences produced on trees, usually the oak species Quercus infectoria in Europe and the Near East, and on the sumac species Rhus semialata in China and Japan, by the action of insects, chiefly of the genus Cynips. Galls are formed when gall-wasp eggs are deposited on tree branches in nut-like pockets; the gall grows until the larvae are completely enveloped. The mature insect bores a hole through the gall in order to escape. All galls contain 36-60% tannins; the bluish-green galls, gathered before the insect escapes, are richest in gallotannic acid. The tannins have been used for centuries for vegetable tanning of leather. When galls are combined with ferrous sulfate, a black dye is produced; alone, they produce a gray dye. Gall extract was also used as a mordant in the preparation of writing inks.  [Source: Getty AAT]

silver leaf.d: Silver beaten out into thin leaf for use in gilding. Silver leaf is about three times as thick as gold leaf because silver is less malleable but the resulting leaf is easier to handle. In the commerical arts inexpensive aluminum leaf is used to achieve the effect of silver leaf. Silver leaf can also be covered with a golden yellow transparent coating as a substitute for gold. carob.d: Species of tree native to the eastern Mediterranean region and cultivated elsewhere. It is highly drought resistant. The tree reaches about 15 m (50 feet) in height, has glossy evergreen leaves, and produces long leathery pods that contain up to 15 hard brown seeds embedded in a sweet, edible pulp. The ripened pods are food for animals and also ground for a variety of uses by humans. The seeds are ground to produce a gum. The seeds were a standard of weight measurement in the ancient world, from which the concept "carat" is derived. The common names referring to locusts or St. John's bread come from the belief that the so-called "locusts" on which John the Baptist fed in the Biblical story were carob pods, not grasshoppers. cremil.d: Refers to a fine, openwork ornamental textile work formed by looping, interlacing, twisting, plaiting, or braiding threads of linen, cotton, silk, hair, metal, or another fiber to form designs or patterns. Lace may be made with a needle or with bobbins. Embroidery may be added. Modern lace may be made by machine. Openwork fabrics made on a loom and ornamental openwork knitting are generally not classified as lace. Lace is often white or monochromatic. True lace developed in the fourteenth century in Europe and the Middle East, although ornamented openwork fabrics were known in ancient cultures, including the Egyptian culture. Lace may be used as a border, edging, or insert on linens or apparel; it is also formed into large pieces of cloth used for hangings, draperies, apparel, or other items.  [Source: Getty AAT]

The blade may be of steel or another metal or stone, as in the flint knives of early man, or of another material such as ivory or wood (as with a paperknife). emerald.d: A brilliant grass-green variety of beryl, highly prized as a gemstone. The name comes indirectly from the Greek "smaragdos," referring to a number of stones having little in common except a green color. The emerald in the the Bible was probably a garnet. However, ancient societies did also value the genuine emerald, which came from Upper Egypt as early as 2000 BCE. Greek emerald miners worked for Alexander the Great and Cleopatra. The physical properties of emerald are essentially the same as those of beryl, with only moderate light refractive and dispersive powers, meaning that cut stones display little brilliancy or fire. The gems are instead valued for their magnificent color, which is probably caused by small amounts of chromium. The stone loses colour when strongly heated. Synthetic emerald was successfully produced in the 1930s, and today is produced by a either a molten-flux process or a hydrothermal method crystal growing process. Synthetic crystals appear very similar to natural emerald crystals. [Source: Getty AAT]

holy water stoup.d: Basins or bowls containing holy water at the entrance of a church. The font may be of various forms, either built into the wall, standing on a pedestal, or as a bucket hanging from a fixture. Often richly decorated, they are typically used by worshippers to cross themselves upon entering and exiting the church. The holy water font evolved from the fountain for ablutions that was placed in the center of the atrium of the early Christian basilica, and is still placed there in Eastern rites. Before entering the church, worshippers washed their hands and feet in accordance with a rite derived from Judaism. When the atrium of the Christian basilica was reduced to the proportions of a narrow court or a simple porch, the fountain gave way to a smaller structure. [Source: Getty AAT]

aspergillum.d: Instruments, usually of metal attached to an absorbent material, for the sprinkling of holy water. In the Western church, the aspergillum is composed of a handle surmounted by a perforated ball, sponge, or brush-like end to hold water. Some have sponges or internal reservoirs that dispense holy water when shaken, while others must periodically be dipped in "aspersoriums (vessels)." The tool was originally made of branches of hyssop, palm, or boxwood, wisps of straw, or the tail of a fox (in Old French the fox was called "goupil"). By the 13th century the aspergillum assumed the modern Western form of a handle surmounted by a rose-shape covered with bristles; the handles of the sprinklers came to be very richly ornamented. In the Greek Orthodox Church the aspergillum is a standing vessel with a tapering lid perforated with holes for sprinkling; in the Russian Orthodox Church, it is a whisk made of cloth, hair, or sprigs of basil. The tool was derived from ancient sources, where branches were used to sprinkle water, blood, or another liquid in rituals. Such tools were used in ancient Rome, the Middle East, ancient Norse rituals, and elsewhere. [Source: Getty AAT]

hair.d: Material comprising the cylindrical filaments that grow from follicles embedded in the skin of mammals. Hair is a column of overlapping, fused cells that are composed of the protein keratin; hair is composed of three parts: the innermost column is the medula, the surrounding live cells (the cortex) contain pigment, and the outermost dead transparent cells are the cuticular scales. The portion of the hair outside of the skin is called the shaft. Fine, closely spaced hair that covers most of an animal's body is called fur. Dense, soft, curled hair is called wool. Coarse, stiff hairs are called bristles, spines, or quills. Horsehair and cattle hair have been used for brushes, plaster binders, haircloth, and upholstery stuffing. Rabbit hair, often called rabbit fur, has been used to make felt hats.  [Source: Getty AAT]

indigo.d: A natural dark blue colorant obtained from the tropical Indigofera tinctoria plants. The use of indigo was first mentioned in Indian manuscripts in the 4th century BCE; it was first exported to Europe in Roman times. The natural material is collected as a precipitate from a fermented solution of the plant, where the coloring component, indigotin, is extracted as a colorless glycoside that turns blue with oxidation. Indigo is a fine, intense powder which may be used directly as a pigment in oil, tempera, or watercolor media. Since the exposed pigment can fade rapidly in strong sunlight, it is rarely used in art or fine textiles today. However, it is still used to dye jeans, where its fading and uneven coloring have become favorable characteristics. [Source: Getty AAT]

lamp.d: Lighting devices having a vessel to contain fuel used as a source of illumination, such as grease or oil. The lamp was invented at least as early as 70,000 BCE, originally consisting of a hollowed-out rock filled with moss or some other absorbent material that was soaked with animal fat and ignited. red lead.d: Heavy, opaque, orange-red pigment composed of lead tetroxide. Although chemically equivalent to the mineral minium, red lead pigment has been synthetically prepared by roasting lead white (480 C) since before the 5th century BCE. Red lead has been found as a pigment on early objects from Egypt, China, Japan, India, Persia, and Rome; it is no longer used as an artist's color because is has poor light stability and poor working properties, although it is still used to color glass and ceramic glazes. Pliny called it "secondarium minium." It was widely used in illuminated manuscripts, and with its use, the term "miniare" came to mean "to color with red lead," giving rise to the term "miniature." Red lead paint was used as an anticorrosion primer for structural iron and steel until the late 20th century. [Source: Getty AAT]

lead.d: Pure metallic element having symbol Pb and atomic number 82; soft, dense ductile metal of a dull gray color, shiny when freshly cut, occuring naturally most often as a sulfide in the mineral galena. Other lead minerals include anglesite (lead sulfate) and cerussite (lead carbonate). Native metallic lead was found and used from about 3600-2600 BCE when the technique for obtaining lead from roasting the sulfide ore (galena) was discovered. Lead was used to make small cast items such as coins and statuettes, plumbing pipes, spires, statues, cisterns, gargoyles, pigments (lead white, litharge, orange mineral, etc.), as a component in pottery glazes, for roofing, flashing, stained glass windows, as a soft solder, and as radiation shielding.
